Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-two years old when he was taken from the street corner where he waited for a ride to his night shift at the automotive parts warehouse in Newark. It was 11:47 p.m. on a November evening, the air cold enough that his breath made small clouds. A van pulled up. Three men. He remembered the one with the scarred face ordering him inside, remembered the weight of hands on his shoulders, the smell of diesel fuel mixed with something chemical and sweet. They kept him in a basement for nine days—no windows, no way to know if it was day or night except by the sounds of traffic above, which came and went in patterns that made no sense to him. They wanted money from his family. His wife Priya had scraped together what she could, borrowed from her brother, and on the tenth morning they let him go.

That was twenty-two years ago. He had returned to work at the warehouse within a month, told people he had been sick, and for two decades had built what felt like a manageable life. But six months ago, something shifted. His younger daughter mentioned snakes in a text message—she was hiking, had seen one on the trail—and Rajesh had felt his chest tighten in a way that surprised him. One of the men in the basement had kept a snake in a terrarium near where they held him. He could still see it, the way it moved, the way the light caught its scales. After that text, he began to notice how often snakes appeared in casual conversation, in nature documentaries that Priya watched, in photographs people shared at work. Each time, his body would flood with the same helpless dread.

The real unraveling began in the evenings. Rajesh had always preferred to stay up late—the night shift had suited him for decades—but now nighttime felt dangerous in a way he could not quite name. He would lie in bed beside Priya and feel his mind cataloguing every sound: the furnace clicking on, a car passing outside, the house settling. By 11:47 p.m., his body would be rigid, waiting. He had come to believe that bad things happened at that hour, that he had no power to prevent them, that if he allowed himself to fall asleep he would be vulnerable to whatever came next. So he stopped sleeping. He would sit in the living room with the television on, or stand at the kitchen window looking out at the street, checking the locks repeatedly, looking behind him as he moved through rooms, certain that someone was there.

Priya grew worried and then frustrated. She would ask him what was wrong, and he would ask her—sometimes five or six times an evening—whether she thought he was okay, whether she was sure he was safe, whether something bad was going to happen. She began to withdraw. His supervisor at the warehouse noticed that Rajesh, once reliable and steady, was making mistakes, moving slowly, seeming distracted. When a coworker mentioned seeing a nature documentary about snakes in the break room, Rajesh felt panic rise in his throat and left his shift early. He called Priya from the car asking if she was home, if the doors were locked, if she was certain he would be alright.

Now, at sixty-four, Rajesh has not had a full night of sleep in six months. He checks his body constantly—his arms, his legs, his chest—looking for signs of injury or illness, convinced that something is wrong with him that he cannot see. He is terrified that if he allows himself to think directly about what happened in that basement, the memory will shatter him completely, that he will not be able to contain it. And underneath all of this runs a darker current: the thought that perhaps his life, stretched out now into this vigilant, fractured existence, is not worth the exhaustion of living it. His daughter finally insisted he see someone, and he came to his first appointment with Priya, exhausted and afraid, hoping that someone could tell him how to feel safe again—or at least, how to stop feeling that safety is something he has already lost forever.
